# Open Source LLMs for Content Analysis

Ready-to-use, open source Large Language Models (LLMs) are an important research infrastructure. They are easy to access, adaptable, scalable, and inexpensive, while achieving a level of performance that can compete with manual content analysis.

This page provides **step-by-step guides** to using these models for content analysis. It is intended as a resource for researchers and practitioners in the social sciences and related fields who are interested in applying LLMs to analyze textual data.

<!-- ## See it in action {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Three model types, three ways to get from raw text to a label — here's the shortest possible taste of each. Full, runnable walkthroughs are in the [Tutorials](sections/tutorials/index.qmd) section.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Category-specific encoder

```python
from transformers import pipeline

classifier = pipeline(
    "text-classification",
    model="SamLowe/roberta-base-go_emotions",
    top_k=None,
)
classifier("I can't stop thinking about what might happen.")
```

Trained once on one fixed set of labels (here: 28 emotion categories) — fast and cheap, but limited to what it was trained on.

## Task-specific encoder

```python
from transformers import pipeline

classifier = pipeline(
    "zero-shot-classification",
    model="MoritzLaurer/deberta-v3-base-zeroshot-v2.0",
)
classifier(
    "I can't stop thinking about what might happen.",
    candidate_labels=["fear", "no fear"],
)
```

Any labels you define yourself, no fine-tuning required — trades a bit of speed for a lot of flexibility.

## Universal decoder

```python
from transformers import pipeline

generate = pipeline("text-generation", model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct")
generate(
    "Does this text express fear? Answer yes or no: "
    "'I can't stop thinking about what might happen.'"
)
```

Free-text output from a generative model — the most flexible option, but it takes care to prompt well and parse the answer.

:::
